cases.abstract: Rotating a manipulation scene changes both the observation and the required gripper motion, but the corresponding transformation depends on whether actions specify absolute poses or relative motions. We introduce Equivariant Diffusion Policy, which encodes this relationship in action denoising. We show that the noise prediction function is equivariant under planar rotations when the expert policy is equivariant, and derive rotation representations for both forms of six-degree-of-freedom control. Equivariant observation and action encoders produce features indexed by discrete rotations; a shared temporal U-Net across those rotations and an equivariant decoder preserve the transformation structure. Across 12 simulated manipulation tasks, the voxel-based policy with absolute control reaches 63.9% average peak success with 100 demonstrations per task, compared with 42.0% for RGB-based standard diffusion policy. Physical-robot evaluation provides a comparison using identical voxel inputs and approximately matched parameter counts: the equivariant policy achieves 80-95% success across six tasks, versus 0-60% for the non-equivariant baseline, using 20-60 demonstrations per task. These results support exploiting rotational structure for data-limited manipulation, while gains with image observations are smaller under relative control.
cases.results: With absolute pose control and 100 demonstrations per task, the image-based equivariant policy achieves 53.7% average success across 12 simulation tasks, versus 42.0% for DiffPo-C using the same temporal U-Net backbone. This comparison supports the utility of the architectural symmetry constraint without introducing voxel observations. The voxel version reaches 72.6% with 200 demonstrations, exceeding the strongest baseline's 71.4% with 1,000 demonstrations, although that comparison also changes the observation representation. Simulation values are peak success rates over 50 evaluations during training, averaged across three seeds. On hardware, both policies receive the same voxel grid and have approximately equal parameter counts. With 40 demonstrations, letter alignment succeeds in 19/20 trials for EquiDiff and 0/20 for the non-equivariant policy. All six hardware tasks favor EquiDiff. The benefits are less pronounced for image-based relative control, where average improvements over the best baseline are 2.1-3.7 percentage points across the tested budgets.

cases.abstract: Re-Mix curates heterogeneous robot demonstration mixtures by learning sampling weights that can be reused across policy training runs without specifying a downstream task. It optimizes worst-case excess imitation loss relative to a reference policy, focusing on domains where the learned policy falls behind the reference rather than on high absolute losses alone. Gaussian action normalization and discretized action likelihoods address mismatched loss scales, multimodal actions, and outlier-sensitive regression losses; validation-based early stopping guards against reference overfitting. The resulting domain weights are transferred to separate diffusion policies, separating data curation from policy architecture. We evaluate on Bridge V2 and the RT-X mixture using WidowX and Franka robots, with local co-training data (25 demonstrations per adaptation task) assigned a total mixture weight of 5%. For RT-X subsets retaining 25% of the data, Re-Mix achieves 80% mean success across four tasks, versus 38% with size-proportional sampling and 33% with expert weights. The two-task full-data Bridge evaluation shows similar performance under Re-Mix and uniform sampling, but quarter-sized subsets favor Re-Mix. These results support action-based curation for the evaluated heterogeneous and data-restricted training settings.
cases.results: At a fixed 25% RT-X data budget, Re-Mix achieves 80% mean success across four hardware tasks, compared with 38% for size-proportional sampling and 33% for expert-defined weights. Final diffusion policies train for 400,000 gradient steps with local demonstrations at 5% mixture weight; each task receives 10 evaluation trials. The comparison therefore measures curation under matched retained-data and training budgets, with learned weights still used for sampling after subsetting. On Bridge, the four-task subset evaluation yields 90% mean success for Re-Mix, versus 50% for uniform sampling and 22% for image-based Self-Supervised Prototypes. In contrast, the two-task full-data Bridge evaluation reports similar performance for learned and uniform weights. The subset comparisons show that retention strategies change downstream performance even at the same data budget. Ablations also link the weighting procedure to its reference: using a checkpoint 50,000 steps after early stopping reduces performance, and replacing discrete actions with continuous actions worsens the subset results.
